3.1.intro: A résumé is a focused record of qualifications relevant to a particular role. In many countries “CV” means much the same thing; in US academic settings a curriculum vitae is usually a longer record of research, teaching and publications. Follow the conventions of the employer and country.
3.1.example: For a retail role, Maya prepares a concise résumé emphasizing service experience. For a university research appointment, a scientist may need a longer academic CV listing publications and presentations.
3.1.watch: A résumé and a CV are not universally different. The name and expected length depend on context.

3.2.intro: A readable résumé helps a busy reader quickly locate relevant information. Common sections include contact details, profile (optional), experience, education, skills and selected projects. Put the most relevant material where the reader can find it. Only include personal details appropriate to the country and role.
3.2.example:
MAYA CHEN · Kyoto | maya@example.com
EXPERIENCE · Store Assistant, 2024–2026
• Helped customers find products and resolved order questions.
EDUCATION · Diploma, 2024
SKILLS · Customer service, spreadsheets, English.
3.2.watch: Do not assume photographs, birth dates or personal information are appropriate everywhere.

3.3.intro: A useful bullet names an action and adds context or a result where possible. Start with a clear verb: coordinated, processed, improved, explained, checked, supported. If you have numbers, use accurate ones; not every contribution can or should be quantified.
3.3.example: Vague: “Responsible for emails.” Specific: “Responded to daily customer emails and tracked unresolved cases for the manager.” The second shows the work without inventing a spectacular metric.
3.3.language: Coordinated weekly schedules for a five-person team.
3.3.watch: Avoid buzzwords without proof and made-up numbers.

3.4.intro: No paid experience does not mean no evidence. School assignments, caregiving, volunteering, independent projects and community work may show relevant skills. Career changes need a clear bridge between past experience and the new job; brief gaps usually need no dramatic explanation.
3.4.example: A student applying for a support role can mention organizing a school event and answering participant questions. Someone moving from hospitality to operations can emphasize scheduling, accurate records and busy-shift coordination.
3.4.language: I am transitioning from hospitality into operations.
3.4.watch: Do not hide limitations with fabricated job titles or invented employment history.

3.5.intro: Use a simple document editor to create your résumé: a clear heading, standard section names, readable spacing and consistent dates. Google Docs, Microsoft Word or LibreOffice can work. Export to the file type the employer asks for and inspect the result before submitting.
3.5.example: Start with a single-column document. Use headings like Experience and Education, then write concise bullets. Save a source copy so you can make targeted versions later.
3.5.language: Attached is my résumé in PDF format.
3.5.watch: Software varies. Avoid assuming every employer's applicant tracking system reads every design equally well.

3.6.intro: Tailoring means making the most relevant true evidence easy to see. Compare your résumé against the job's actual duties, then change the order and phrasing where appropriate. You are not trying to trick a robot; you are helping a person or system interpret accurate information.
3.6.example: If the advertisement stresses order tracking, Maya moves her record-keeping experience higher. She does not add a software skill she has never used just because it appears in the posting.
3.6.language: Maintained accurate order records during busy shifts.
3.6.watch: Keyword stuffing and decorative layouts can reduce clarity; simple formatting is a sensible default, not a magic guarantee.

3.7.intro: You now have enough information to build a first usable draft. Choose a format appropriate to your role, include only truthful evidence, and check the document against a real advertisement. A draft is a working document, not a judgment of your worth.
3.7.example: Starter résumé: Name and contact; relevant experience or projects; education; skills. Experienced résumé: Name; relevant experience with clear achievements; selected education; skills. Academic CV: education, research experience, publications and presentations as relevant.
3.7.watch: Keep a master copy plus tailored versions. Remove private information before sharing your draft publicly.

4.1.intro: A cover letter is a short explanation of why this particular role and your evidence belong together. It supplements, rather than repeats, the résumé. Some applications require it; some do not accept one at all. The employer's instructions come first.
4.1.example: A résumé lists that Maya handled customer requests. Her letter explains that this experience matches Northstar's need for careful case follow-up.
4.1.language: I am applying for the Customer Support Assistant position.
4.1.watch: A long, generic letter can be worse than a focused, relevant one.

4.2.intro: Imagine you are the reader: you need to know what role this person wants, what evidence they bring and why that evidence matters to your team's work. Answer these questions quickly. You do not need theatrical enthusiasm or compliments.
4.2.example: An unhelpful opening praises Northstar as “the greatest organization in the world.” A useful opening states the role and connects a relevant experience to the team's work.
4.2.language: Your advertisement emphasizes accurate communication; that matches my experience with customer requests.
4.2.watch: The reader does not need your full biography or explanations for every life decision.

4.3.intro: A simple structure is enough: identify the role and reason for applying; give one or two relevant examples; connect them to the employer's needs; close with thanks and a clear next step. Adjust the order if the situation calls for it.
4.3.example:
Hello Hiring Team,
I'm applying for the Support Assistant role at Northstar. In my last position I answered customer questions and logged unresolved cases for follow-up. Your team needs accurate, patient communication, and that is work I enjoy. I'd welcome a conversation about the role.
Kind regards,
Maya Chen
4.3.language: I'd welcome the opportunity to discuss how I could contribute.
4.3.watch: Three paragraphs are a useful example, not a law. Follow any explicit length or format requirement.

4.4.intro: A strong letter is specific enough that the reader can see the connection. Replace empty claims such as “I am passionate and hardworking” with experience. Clear English is more persuasive than inflated vocabulary. Address gaps briefly and honestly if relevant.
4.4.example: Weak: “I know I am a perfect candidate.” Better: “I regularly answered customer questions and passed complex issues to my supervisor, which matches the support duties in your advertisement.”
4.4.language: That experience would help me contribute to ...
4.4.watch: Do not fabricate achievements, overflatter the company or apologize for your whole background.

4.5.intro: Before sending an application, confirm the correct employer, role and submission channel. Check filenames, attachment versions, contact information, eligibility answers and deadlines. Follow the stated instructions. A short application email should make it easy to find the materials.
4.5.example:
Subject: Application — Support Assistant — Maya Chen
Hello Hiring Team,
Please find my résumé and cover letter attached for the Support Assistant role. Thank you for considering my application.
Kind regards,
Maya Chen
4.5.language: Please find my résumé and cover letter attached.
4.5.watch: A missing attachment or incorrect role name can undo careful preparation. Always preview the final submission.

4.6.intro: Compose a letter for one specific vacancy using the evidence you selected earlier. Write plainly, then revise for accuracy, relevance and length. Ask: Does every paragraph help the reader decide whether to speak with me? If not, cut or rewrite it.
4.6.example: Draft around four questions: Which role? Why this opportunity? What did you do that supports your fit? What is the next step? Compare your draft with the Northstar example, but keep your own facts.
4.6.language: I would welcome the chance to explain my experience further.
4.6.watch: Your letter should sound like a real applicant, not a template filled with invented passion.
